transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-22 16:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes (approx)
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Daniel Ortiz (Redwood SE), Connor Li (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Bluewave CTO), Liam O'Connor (Bluewave ML Eng), Marco Ruiz (Bluewave Head Infra), Sara Feldman (Product)

Summary: quick workshop to lock acceptance guardrails, concrete success thresholds for the POC, workload sizing, and exact reporting format for the benchmark deliverable. Aim is to have a clear go/no-go checklist and spreadsheet that both sides can sign off on before running the benchmark.

Topics covered: Success criteria (latency, quality, cost), workload definition (QPS, sequence lengths, traffic shape), acceptance tests (pass/fail thresholds, noise handling), reporting artifacts (CSV formats, dashboards, raw logs), timeline and owners.

[00:00:12] Maya (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I think we have about 50 minutes, we'll run through the acceptance guardrails and then leave time for Qs and to confirm next steps.
[00:00:28] Priya (CTO): Thanks Maya. We want the bench to be defensible — execs want clear pass/fail. So, thresholds that are measurable and reproducible.
[00:00:43] Daniel (SE): Totally. We'll propose a two-tier acceptance: core functional (quality metrics) and operational (latency, throughput, error rate, cost per 1k tokens). If either tier fails the go criteria we flag it as no-go.
[00:01:05] Liam (ML): Quick clarification — when you say "quality metrics" do you mean F1/EM style or something like BLEU/ROUGE? Our use case is entity extraction + slot filling, so F1 on labeled entities is best.
[00:01:22] Maya: Yes, entity F1 for primary metric. We'll accept secondary metrics like exact match for end-to-end response when available.
[00:01:37] Marco (Infra): For operational we need p95 latency under 220ms for 1.5k QPS sustained during the 1-hour peak window. If that can't be met we'd need a fallback plan.
[00:01:52] Connor (SE): Noted. Marco can you confirm typical request/sequence length distribution? That impacts batching and kernel choices.
[00:02:06] Marco: Right now 70% of requests are short (avg 32 tokens input, 64 tokens output), 20% mid (150/200 tokens), 10% long tails up to 1k. Peak sustained QPS around 1.5k internally but burst could hit 4k for <10m.
[00:02:30] Daniel: Perfect, we'll include a synthetic workload that matches that distribution plus a tail stress run to validate burst behavior.
[00:02:45] Priya: On quality thresholds — baseline internal model is F1 0.87. Our ask is that Redwood's serving of the chosen model meets F1 >= 0.89 on the 10k testset to be a pass. Anything below 0.86 is auto-fail. Between 0.86 and 0.89 is 'amber' and requires remediation.
[00:03:10] Maya: We'll capture those as explicit gates in the spreadsheet. For operational: p50 < 60ms, p95 < 220ms for the core route. Error rate (5xx) must be <0.1% over the run. Cost target is less prescriptive but we'd like to see token cost per 1k under $12 for the pilot.
[00:03:35] Sara (Product): Can you define "core route"? We have three endpoints: fast-response routing, longform helper, and embeddings.
[00:03:47] Daniel: We'll treat the fast-response API (short seq) as core. Longform gets separate acceptance thresholds (p95 < 900ms) and embeddings are measured by throughput (reqs/sec) rather than single-request latency.
[00:04:03] Liam: For the dataset we'll give you 10k labeled queries with golden entity labels. We'll also attach a 1k validation holdout.
[00:04:15] Maya: Great — that's exactly what we need. We'll ask Bluewave to provide label format: CSV columns [id, input_text, labels_json, route].
[00:04:29] Priya: About randomness — we need runs to be reproducible. How do you handle random seed, KV cache warmup, and cold-start artifacts?
[00:04:44] Daniel: Good question. The runbook will lock seeds and warm the KV cache with a 30-minute synthetic warmup pass. We'll do three measurement windows and report median values. We'll also include raw logs with timestamps so you can rerun analyses.
[00:05:02] Marco: We need to ensure the private deployment path remains available as an option if hosted can't meet the latency. Any differences in acceptance criteria if it's Dedicated or Private?
[00:05:15] Maya: Acceptance thresholds remain the same; we just note that deployment mode may change costs and provisioning times. Dedicated will have more predictable throughput so it's often easier to pass p95 SLOs. We'll add a line item in the spreadsheet to record deployment mode used in each run.
[00:05:31] Connor: Also we'll log CPU/GPU utilization, memory, and eviction stats per node; those are helpful for postmortem.
[00:05:42] Liam: For quality gating — do you compute entity-level F1 only, or also a human-curated hallucination rate? We care about hallucination for specific sensitive entities.
[00:05:55] Daniel: We'll include a simple hallucination metric: fraction of entity outputs not present in input or golden labels, flagged for manual review. That sits alongside F1 in the spreadsheet.
[00:06:09] Priya: Let's write down exact pass/fail logic now so there's no ambiguity.
[00:06:14] Maya: Proposal (we'll put into the sheet):
- Quality tier (pass): entity F1 >= 0.89 on the 10k testset AND hallucination rate < 2%
- Quality tier (fail): entity F1 < 0.86 OR hallucination rate > 5%
- Operational tier (pass): p95 latency < 220ms on core route, error rate <0.1%, and sustained throughput within 10% of requested QPS profile during measurement windows
- Operational tier (fail): p95 >= 300ms OR error rate > 0.5% OR inability to sustain peak bursts without >1% dropped requests
- Overall go: both tiers pass. Amber requires mitigation plan and re-run.
[00:07:05] Marco: That looks reasonable. I want to add an availability gate: no more than 2 minutes of total downtime during the bench run.
[00:07:14] Maya: Noted, we'll add availability as an operational sub-check.
[00:07:20] Sara: Reporting format — what exactly will you hand off?
[00:07:25] Connor: Deliverables we'll provide: (1) CSV with per-request results (id, input, output, latency_ms, error_flag, entity_matches, hallucination_flag), (2) aggregated metrics sheet with p50/p95/p99, F1, hallucination, cost calc, (3) a short PDF executive summary, (4) a raw log tarball and the benchmark runbook.
[00:07:45] Liam: CSV format okay but we need to ensure PII is redacted. We'll scrub identifiers from the shared CSV.
[00:07:53] Daniel: We'll sign an ephemeral data transfer agreement for the dataset and delete after runs if you prefer. We'll note KMS usage for any private deployments.
[00:08:05] Priya: Security docs — can you send SOC2 and any infra network diagrams? Marco will take a look.
[00:08:12] Maya: Yes, we'll attach SOC2 summary and our dedicated VPC architecture diagram to the follow-up email.
[00:08:20] Priya: For the reporting cadence — we expect a runbook + raw outputs within 48 hours of the run, summary slides within 72 hours.
[00:08:29] Maya: That's fair. We'll aim for same-day raw CSV if possible but 48 hours is our commitment.
[00:08:35] Connor: On benchmarking mechanics, we'll run three warmup phases: cache warmup (30 min), nominal pass (1 hour at the requested QPS mix), tail stress (20 minutes full burst), and a cleanup. Each measurement window will be timeboxed and repeated three times.
[00:08:54] Marco: What about synthetic vs replay workload? Replay gives more realism but needs sanitized logs.
[00:09:02] Daniel: We prefer replay where possible because it preserves request correlations; if you can't share logs we'll generate synthetic workloads matching your token-length distribution and traffic envelope.
[00:09:14] Sara: Timeline — when can we expect the first baseline run?
[00:09:18] Maya: If we get the dataset by 2026-07-24, we can stand up the test environment and schedule the baseline run for 2026-07-29, with results out by 2026-07-31. Optimization and follow-up runs could occur the following week.
[00:09:33] Priya: That aligns with our internal roadmap. We want a final go/no-go decision by 2026-08-07 so we can coordinate procurement if positive.
[00:09:43] Maya: Understood — we'll target that.
[00:09:47] Liam: One more detail — do you include cost modeling for both hosted and dedicated? We need a cost-per-QPS projection over 3 sizing scenarios.
[00:09:57] Maya: Yes, we'll include a simple cost projection: baseline hosted per-token cost observed in the run, plus an estimated dedicated monthly cost (based on reserved GPU pool) at three utilization bands (40/70/95%). We'll attach a spreadsheet tab with assumptions.
[00:10:11] Priya: Good. Also add a sensitivity column for sequence length since that changes effective throughput.
[00:10:18] Daniel: We'll capture that.
[00:10:22] Connor: On CI — we can also provide a tiny harness so you can re-run a subset daily to guard against regressions. Not part of the POC pass/fail but useful.
[00:10:32] Priya: We'll take that.
[00:10:35] Maya: Okay we're about halfway. Any outstanding unknowns?
[00:10:40] Marco: A small note on network egress/residency: if we run hosted in us-west and your control plane is elsewhere, we need to validate routing. We'll add a network test as part of baseline.
[00:10:51] Daniel: We'll include an end-to-end network trace and region used in the report.
[00:10:56] Liam: For the acceptance rubric, can you add a clause for partial acceptance where specific routes pass but others don't? For example, if core route passes but longform fails we might still go forward with a limited rollout.
[00:11:09] Maya: We'll include route-level pass/fail and an overall recommendation. We'll surface any mitigations and a go/no-go recommendation tied to risk tolerance.
[00:11:18] Priya: Let's capture the exact CSV column names now so there are no later mismatches.
[00:11:22] Connor: Proposed columns: request_id, timestamp_utc, route, input_token_count, output_token_count, latency_ms, status_code, error_message, entities_expected, entities_returned, entity_f1, hallucination_flag, cost_tokens, run_id.
[00:11:40] Liam: Fine, please add a column for model_version and quantization_profile.
[00:11:46] Daniel: Added.
[00:11:49] Maya: Great.
[00:11:52] Priya: On signoff — do you want an email confirmation from us or a short 15-minute review meeting after the run?
[00:11:58] Maya: Let's plan a 30-minute readout for the baseline results and signoff — that gives time for questions. We'll schedule it for 48-72 hours after the run.
[00:12:07] Marco: If the baseline is amber, that 30-minute readout should include remediation plan and timeline.
[00:12:13] Sara: Anything else on acceptance thresholds? I'm thinking about dataset noise — sometimes labels are inconsistent, that can affect F1. How will you handle label noise?
[00:12:23] Daniel: We'll run an inter-annotator agreement pass on a 500-sample subset to estimate label noise and surface it. If noise exceeds 4% we'll flag the quality numbers as lower confidence and both sides will agree whether to proceed.
[00:12:40] Priya: Good guardrail.
[00:12:43] Maya: Okay quick recap and owners — I'll read items then you confirm.
[00:12:48] Maya: Action items: Redwood sends benchmark runbook + CSV and spreadsheet template (Maya) due 2026-07-27; Bluewave provides 10k labeled queries + 1k holdout and anonymized logs (Liam) due 2026-07-24; Redwood prepares provisioning script for dedicated trial (Daniel) due 2026-07-30; schedule baseline run week of 2026-07-29 (all). Any objections?
[00:13:14] Priya: No objections. Sounds good.
[00:13:17] Marco: I'll review the SOC2 docs once you send and confirm any network constraints.
[00:13:22] Maya: We'll send everything after the call.
[00:13:25] Connor: One last note on measurement reproducibility — we'll include the exact container image SHA, model binary hash, and config used.
[00:13:33] Liam: Excellent.
[00:13:36] Priya: Thank you all, that was productive.
[00:13:40] Maya: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the artifacts and calendar invites.
